name: Ho Chi Minh City food guide
summary: Ho Chi Minh City mixes plates from many regions. Vietnam Tourism says hủ tiếu is the bowl that is best here, and that phở is best in Hanoi. A later page still describes a sweeter southern phở, and names bánh tráng trộn, bún bò Nam Bộ, xôi, and chè beside cơm tấm, bánh mì, and bánh xèo. Cơm tấm, hủ tiếu, bánh mì, bánh xèo, gỏi cuốn, and cà phê sữa đá are the plates with a photograph.
body: Vietnam Tourism sets the two cities apart: Hanoi food is described as more delicate and lighter on seasoning, and this city as a place that mixes ingredients and recipes from many regions. What was born here is still best here. Phở is best in Hanoi, and Vietnam Tourism uses that to point you at hủ tiếu.

The delicious-dishes page, drawn from more than 104,000 votes for the city’s “100 interesting things” list, still names phở here and splits the bowl. Northern-style restaurants have a light, clear, less sweet broth. The southern bowl is sweeter, and darker from grilled purple onions and spices, with bean sprouts, raw vegetables, sliced onions, garlic, and soy sauce. Visit HCMC and the national attractions page also name phở. Named shops are doors a page used to locate a plate. A stall price on those pages is not the city price.
specialtiesLead: The plates with a photograph are cơm tấm, hủ tiếu, bánh mì, bánh xèo, gỏi cuốn, and cà phê sữa đá. Bánh tráng trộn, bún bò Nam Bộ, xôi, and chè are named on the delicious-dishes page. The other plates are named for this city too.

sections.heading: Regional dishes
paragraphs: The plates below are also named for this city. Phở is one of them. Vietnam Tourism’s cuisine page says it is best in Hanoi and points you at hủ tiếu. The delicious-dishes page names bánh tráng trộn, bún bò Nam Bộ, the Hue bowl as it is eaten here, xôi, and a long list of chè, and it still describes a southern phở. Visit HCMC lists phở bò on Bùi Viện. Where the pages disagree, both stay.

spots.name: Oc
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism calls snails one of the city’s specialties. Restaurants lay the day’s catch in baskets, up to twenty kinds, and names sweet snails, cockles, and razor clams, stir-fried with butter and garlic, grilled with sea salt and chili, or stewed in coconut milk. A later page says they are boiled, steamed, grilled, or sautéed and eaten from the shell with a cold beer. The delicious-dishes page says they are steamed, boiled, stir-fried, roasted, or grilled, and that boiled snails are dipped in ginger chilli sauce, salted egg, or tamarind sauce. It also names oysters, crabs, sentinel crabs, prawn, and squid at that evening snack. The city itinerary’s District 4 spread adds crab, scallops, molluscs, and freshwater snails in butter, garlic, lemongrass, and chili. The lists do not match. All of them stay. Vĩnh Khánh comes to life around 6 p.m.

spots.name: Bun thit nuong
spots.note: The city itinerary names grilled pork noodle bowls on afternoon sidewalk stalls next to cơm tấm. No ingredient list beyond that name. The street was not named. Check on arrival.

spots.name: Banh beo
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism’s feast-streets page: translucent morsels filled with shrimp and pork, often eight to ten in an order, for sharing. No dipping sauce was named on that page. Visit HCMC’s Ben Thanh page says the market’s steamed rice cakes come with a special sauce and calls the taste savory. A price on that page is a market figure, not the city price. This is not the Hue recipe.

spots.name: Banh cuon
spots.note: The same feast-streets page: steamed rice rolls with mushrooms, black fungus, and ground pork, meant to be shared.

spots.name: Bo la lot
spots.note: The feast-streets page: marinated beef in piper lolot leaves, with rice noodles, fresh herbs, and rice paper. You roll them yourself and dip in fish sauce.

spots.name: Bo kho
spots.note: The feast-streets page: beef stew, chunks of beef, vegetables, chili, and lime, served with a fresh roll.

spots.name: Banh canh cua
spots.note: The feast-streets page: a seafood soup with crab, shrimp, and rice or tapioca noodles in a pork broth. Visit HCMC names stall 1301 at Ben Thanh for this bowl, with fresh toppings and a hearty broth.

spots.name: Banh da xuc hen
spots.note: The feast-streets page: tiny fried clams with lemongrass, chili, onion, garlic, and coriander, peanuts, and a few sesame crackers. It is not bánh đa cua.

spots.name: Pha lau
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism names phá lấu as a Ho Chi Minh City staple on Hồ Thị Kỷ, in the same sentence as tamarind-seed sweet soup. No ingredient list was printed.

spots.name: Tamarind-seed sweet soup
spots.note: Named on Hồ Thị Kỷ on the same Vietnam Tourism page, as a specialty beside phá lấu. No Vietnamese name and no method were printed.

spots.name: Bun Thai
spots.note: Named at alley 76 of Hai Bà Trưng as a hot meal at the afternoon peak, 15:00–18:00. No recipe was printed.

spots.name: Bun rieu
spots.note: Named at alley 76 in the same sentence as bún Thái, chicken and rice, grilled skewers, and bột chiên. No recipe was printed for that alley bowl. Visit HCMC’s Ben Thanh page says the bowl is crab meat, pork blood curd, and tofu in a rich broth.

spots.name: Chicken and rice
spots.note: Named at alley 76 as a hearty late lunch or early dinner. No Vietnamese name and no method were printed.

spots.name: Grilled skewers
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism says the skewers at alley 76 are cooked to order, hot off the barbecue. No meat was named.

spots.name: Bot chien
spots.note: Fried dough bites served with egg and shredded papaya, named at alley 76 as an alternative to noodles.

spots.name: Mangosteen chicken salad
spots.note: Visit HCMC names mangosteen chicken salad in one list with bánh mì, phở, and cơm tấm. No Vietnamese name, no method, and no street were printed.

spots.name: Stingray hotpot
spots.note: Visit HCMC names stingray hotpot in that same sentence. No Vietnamese name and no method were printed.

spots.name: Pho
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism’s cuisine page says phở is the national soup and is best in Hanoi, and points a reader in this city toward hủ tiếu. The delicious-dishes page describes two bowls in this city: northern-style restaurants with a light, clear, less sweet broth, and a southern bowl that is sweeter, with a darker broth from grilled purple onions and spices, served with bean sprouts, raw vegetables, sliced onions, garlic, and soy sauce. Visit HCMC still names phở bò on Bùi Viện, and the welcome page lists phở with bánh mì and cơm tấm as an iconic dish. Both accounts stay.

spots.name: Banh trang tron
spots.note: A snack, not a main course, on Vietnam Tourism’s delicious-dishes page. Rice paper dried in dew and cut small, mixed with shredded green mango, finely chopped laksa leaves, Tay Ninh shrimp salt, and kumquat juice, then fried onion fat with peanuts, roasted shrimp, quail eggs, and beef jerky. The page names Turtle Lake, Nguyễn Thượng Hiền in District 3, September 23 Park in District 1, the Ben Thanh area, and the corner of Nguyễn Thái Học and Trần Hưng Đạo in District 1. A shop hour was not printed. Check on arrival.

spots.name: Bun bo Nam Bo
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism’s delicious-dishes page calls this a popular southern dish, unlike the Hue bowl. It is brothless, with small rice vermicelli, a spicy and sour chilli-garlic fish sauce, and thinly sliced stir-fried beef. Herbs named: bean sprouts, cucumbers, fried shallots, and roasted peanuts. A street was not printed. Check on arrival.

spots.name: Bun bo Hue
spots.note: The delicious-dishes page says Hue spicy beef rice vermicelli followed Hue people to this city. The bowl it describes looks fuller than in Hue: more meat and rolls, a rich spicy broth, beef with pork sausage, and fresh vegetables. The broth has a sweet taste of sugar, which the page says reduces the strong smell of shrimp paste. The page says Anthony Bourdain once recognized the Hue bowl as one of the most delicious dishes in the world. Bún bò Nam Bộ on the same page is the brothless southern plate. A street in this city was not printed. Check on arrival.

spots.name: Sweet sticky rice
spots.note: Vendors on the delicious-dishes page sell meat sticky rice and sweet sticky rice in the morning, at noon, in the afternoon, in the evening, and late at night. Sweet options named: beans, durian, corn, and sweet gourd. The typical plate is a layer of soft, hot sticky rice, a little grated coconut, then granulated sugar and roasted peanuts. Corn sticky rice is the next plate, with its own method. A shop street was not printed. Check on arrival.

spots.name: Corn sticky rice
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism calls this one of the typical sweet sticky rice dishes: sticky corn stewed with coconut water until the seeds are soft and bright white. The page says it is a bit mushy, and sweet but not greasy. When eating, add a little grated coconut, sugar, and peanuts or sesame salt.

spots.name: Cade sticky rice
spots.note: The delicious-dishes page calls this a more southern style. Soft, chewy sticky rice is stuffed into fresh banana leaves and topped with a soft layer of cadé made from coconut milk, eggs, flour, and sugar.

spots.name: Meat sticky rice
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism’s delicious-dishes page serves meat sticky rice in this city with xa xiu (roasted pork), dried shrimp, sausage, meat floss, pork rolls, and quail eggs, plus fatty onions or fried shallots, and a rich sauce.

spots.name: Chicken sticky rice
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism’s delicious-dishes page serves chicken sticky rice as marinated chicken thighs, onion fat, pickled mustard greens, and a cooked sauce. Side dishes named: crispy fried chicken skin, eggs, shredded chicken, shumai, and boiled gizzard liver. This is sticky rice. The chicken and rice at alley 76, on the cuisine page, had no Vietnamese name.

spots.name: Lotus-seed sweet soup
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism’s delicious-dishes page names lotus seed among the sweet soups in Ho Chi Minh City. Shops are along streets in Districts 1, 5, and 10. A method for this bowl was not printed. Check on arrival.

spots.name: Green-bean sweet soup
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism’s delicious-dishes page names green beans among the city’s sweet soups. The Su Van Hanh tray also has a regular sweet soup made from beans, and a white-bean cup. The page does not say these are one bowl. A method for green beans was not printed. Check on arrival.

spots.name: Red-bean sweet soup
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism’s delicious-dishes page names red beans among the city’s sweet soups, separate from the bean cup on the Su Van Hanh tray. A method was not printed. Shops are along streets in Districts 1, 5, and 10. Check on arrival.

spots.name: Peanut sweet soup
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism’s delicious-dishes page names peanuts among the city’s sweet soups. A method was not printed. Shops are along streets in Districts 1, 5, and 10. Check on arrival.

spots.name: Black-sesame sweet soup
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism’s delicious-dishes page names black sesame among the city’s sweet soups. A method was not printed. Shops are along streets in Districts 1, 5, and 10. Check on arrival.

spots.name: Longan sweet soup
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism’s delicious-dishes page names longan among the city’s sweet soups. A method was not printed. Shops are along streets in Districts 1, 5, and 10. Check on arrival.

spots.name: Ginkgo sweet soup
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism’s delicious-dishes page names ginkgo among the city’s sweet soups. A method was not printed. Shops are along streets in Districts 1, 5, and 10. Check on arrival.

spots.name: Water-chestnut sweet soup
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism’s delicious-dishes page names water chestnut among the city’s sweet soups. A method was not printed. Shops are along streets in Districts 1, 5, and 10. Check on arrival.

spots.name: Ginseng-tonic sweet soup
spots.note: The delicious-dishes page names ginseng tonic among the city’s sweet soups. A method was not printed. Shops are along streets in Districts 1, 5, and 10. Check on arrival.

spots.name: Braised chicken egg
spots.note: The delicious-dishes page names braised chicken egg, like flan, among the city’s sweet soups. The Su Van Hanh tray also lists a plate of flan. The page does not say they are the same. A method was not printed. Check on arrival.

spots.name: Chicken egg soaked in black tea
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism’s delicious-dishes page names chicken egg soaked in black tea among the city’s sweet soups. A method was not printed. Shops are along streets in Districts 1, 5, and 10. Check on arrival.

spots.name: Steamed-papaya sweet soup
spots.note: The delicious-dishes page names steamed papaya among the city’s sweet soups. A method was not printed. Shops are along streets in Districts 1, 5, and 10. Check on arrival.

spots.name: Ba Ba sweet soup
spots.note: One cup on the 16-cup tray at the sweet-soup shop on Su Van Hanh, which the delicious-dishes page points to for southern flavours. The shop was not named. A method for Ba Ba was not printed. Check on arrival.

spots.name: Regular bean sweet soup
spots.note: On the Su Van Hanh tray, the page calls this the regular sweet soup and says it is made from beans. The city list also names green beans and red beans, and the tray names white bean. The page does not say these are one bowl. Check on arrival.

spots.name: Banana sweet soup
spots.note: Named on the 16-cup tray at the unnamed sweet-soup shop on Su Van Hanh. A method was not printed. Check on arrival.

spots.name: Corn sweet soup
spots.note: Named on the Su Van Hanh tray. This is a sweet soup, not the corn sticky rice above. A method was not printed. Check on arrival.

spots.name: White-bean sweet soup
spots.note: Named on the Su Van Hanh tray, beside the regular bean sweet soup. The page does not say it is the green-bean or red-bean bowl. A method was not printed. Check on arrival.

spots.name: Taro sweet soup
spots.note: Named on the Su Van Hanh tray. A method was not printed. The shop was not named. Check on arrival.

spots.name: Dumplings sweet soup
spots.note: Named on the Su Van Hanh tray. A method was not printed. The shop was not named. Check on arrival.

spots.name: Thai sweet soup
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism says the city has a street that sells Thai sweet soup. The street is not named. The page says the flavour is durian, with a sweet and fatty milk taste. Check on arrival.

spots.name: Flan
spots.note: The Su Van Hanh tray comes with a plate of flan, a jar of coconut jelly, and a plate of sticky rice. Braised chicken egg is a separate name on the same page, described as like flan. The page does not say the plate and the egg are the same dessert. The shop was not named.

sections.heading: International dining
paragraphs: Vietnam Tourism says the stalls on Bùi Viện serve Vietnamese street food and also Indian, Italian, Chinese, and Thai food. No shop name was printed for those four kitchens. They are the street’s kitchens, not a ranked list. Quince and Baozi are in Fine dining, which is the chapter that named them.

spots.name: Indian kitchens on Bui Vien
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism names Indian food among the stalls and rooms on Bùi Viện. No restaurant name was printed. The street was made the city’s second official walking street in 2017. Eating starts around dinner and continues all night.

spots.name: Italian kitchens on Bui Vien
spots.note: Italian food is named on the same page, on the same street. No restaurant name was printed.

spots.name: Chinese kitchens on Bui Vien
spots.note: Chinese food is named on the same page, on the same street. No restaurant name was printed. This is not the unnamed Chinatown street in District 5.

spots.name: Thai kitchens on Bui Vien
spots.note: Thai food is named on the same page, on the same street. No restaurant name was printed.

sections.heading: Casual dining
paragraphs: These are the streets and the doors the city pages name for everyday eating. A door is a place a page used to locate a plate. It is not a rank. Where a page printed a stall figure, that figure stays off this page.

spots.name: Ben Thanh food end
spots.address: 32-30 Phan Bội Châu, Ben Thanh, District 1
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism says the end of the hall is a maze of stalls cooking bánh xèo and assembling bánh mì. The market faces Quách Thị Trang. The clock printed there is a repeated block used on several sights. Hours: Check on arrival.

spots.name: Vinh Khanh
spots.note: After dark, snails and seafood. Vietnam Tourism says the street comes to life around 6 p.m. on weekdays and weekends, and that people grill meat and seafood on coal at the table. A closing hour was not printed.

spots.name: Nhieu Loc bank
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism sends you to the restaurants along this canal, a branch of the Saigon River, for the same snail-and-seafood evening. A separate clock was not printed.

spots.name: Co Giang
spots.note: A Vietnamese street-food stretch at the edge of a block of bars, with barbecue, fryers, and steam under fluorescent lights. No clock was printed.

spots.name: Tran Khac Chan
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism calls it a neon strip of eating options, cars and motorbikes mixed with people on foot. No clock was printed.

spots.name: Phan Van Han
spots.note: A neighborhood lane at the edge of District 1, for students and locals, sidewalk tables, bare bulbs. No clock was printed.

spots.name: Nguyen Thuong Hien
spots.note: Sidewalk dining: clams, sea snails, crab claws, oysters, fruit juice, and beer, and diners singing with guitar players. The page does not call this the cơm tấm street.

spots.name: Ho Thi Ky
spots.note: A few hundred meters of food and drink stalls beside the flower wholesale market. Flower trucks come from Đà Lạt and nearby provinces. On the stalls: noodle soups, snails, fruit, cakes, phá lấu, and tamarind-seed sweet soup. Students and workers come after class. A clock was not printed.

spots.name: Alley 76 Hai Ba Trung
spots.note: Smaller than Hồ Thị Kỷ. The peak is 15:00–18:00. The page says this is a hot meal: bún Thái, bún riêu, chicken and rice, grilled skewers, and bột chiên with egg and shredded papaya. A full open and close were not printed.

spots.name: Bui Vien
spots.address: About 850 m, crossing Đề Thám, Phạm Ngũ Lão, and Đỗ Quang Đẩu
spots.note: Vietnamese stalls, barbecue with beer, bánh mì, phở bò, and seafood. Visit HCMC says the street never sleeps. Vietnam Tourism says dinner time and then all night. The Indian, Italian, Chinese, and Thai kitchens are in International dining.

spots.name: A Chinatown food street
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism says the Chinatown street is lined with food stalls, cafes, and bars. It never names the street. No name is added here.

spots.name: Van Kiep
spots.address: The border of Phú Nhuận and Bình Thạnh
spots.note: Neon signs and a run of Vietnamese dishes, a young crowd. The page says a rare dish is what the street is for, and does not name that dish.

spots.name: Com tam Ba Ghien
spots.note: The door Vietnam Tourism names when it tells you to use the nearest cơm tấm room. The plate is the specialty page.

spots.name: Oc Vu
spots.note: Named on Vĩnh Khánh for the snail evening. No menu beyond the street’s baskets was printed.

spots.name: Oc Oanh
spots.note: The city itinerary names this door for crab, scallops, molluscs, and freshwater snails in butter, garlic, lemongrass, and chili.

spots.name: Hu tieu Ba Hoang
spots.note: The door Vietnam Tourism names for hủ tiếu. The bowl is the specialty page.

spots.name: Banh mi Huynh Hoa
spots.note: Named for bánh mì. The same page prints a figure for that shop. That figure is not the city price, so it is not printed here. The delicious-dishes page names the shop among bakeries that have existed for more than half a century.

spots.name: Banh mi Hoa Ma
spots.note: Visit HCMC names Bánh mì Hoa Mã on Bùi Viện. No street number was printed. The delicious-dishes page names it among bakeries that have existed for more than half a century.

spots.name: Goi cuon Minh
spots.note: The door Vietnam Tourism names for gỏi cuốn, with iced tea after a walk.

spots.name: Cuc Gach Quan
spots.note: The city itinerary calls it a family-style restaurant in a beautiful old house. No street was printed.

spots.name: Quan Bui
spots.note: The city itinerary names Quán Bụi for a Vietnamese dinner. No street was printed. The page does not call it fine dining.

spots.name: Ben Thanh night market
spots.address: Phan Chu Trinh and Phan Bội Châu, beside Ben Thanh
spots.note: Visit HCMC says the night market starts at 7:00 PM, with over 100 stalls along those streets. The food it names is seafood and grilled dishes. It does not name the seafood or the grill. A closing hour was not printed. Check on arrival.

spots.name: Bay Ho Bakery
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism’s delicious-dishes page names Bay Ho Bakery among bánh mì shops that have existed for more than half a century. No street was printed. Fillings it names for the city loaf: shumai, pork skin, fish cake, roasted pork, grilled beef, and shredded chicken.

spots.name: Tang banh mi
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism’s delicious-dishes page names this bakery among bánh mì shops that have existed for more than half a century. No street was printed.

spots.name: Cu Ly banh mi
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism’s delicious-dishes page names this bakery among bánh mì shops that have existed for more than half a century. No street was printed.

spots.name: Sau Le banh mi
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism’s delicious-dishes page names this bakery among bánh mì shops that have existed for more than half a century. No street was printed.

spots.name: Su Van Hanh sweet soup
spots.note: The delicious-dishes page sends you here for sweet soup with southern flavours. The shop is not named. The tray is 16 cups: Ba Ba, a bean sweet soup, banana, corn, white bean, taro, and dumplings, with a jar of coconut jelly, a plate of sticky rice, and a plate of flan.

spots.name: A Thai sweet soup street
spots.note: Vietnam Tourism says the city has a street specialising in Thai sweet soup. It never names the street. The bowl smells of durian and tastes of sweet, fatty milk.

spots.name: Che Be
spots.address: Stall 1154–1130, West Side, Gate 7, Ben Thanh, Phan Chu Trinh, District 1
spots.note: Visit HCMC calls this the renowned chè stall in Ben Thanh, with over 40 years specialising in southern-style chè. The cups in the glass cases are not named. A price was not printed.

sections.heading: Fine dining
paragraphs: These three names are the fine-dining chapter on Vietnam Tourism. Visit HCMC also says the city has Michelin-recognised restaurants. That sentence names no door, so no further name is added. No price was printed for these rooms.

spots.name: Quince Saigon
spots.note: Mediterranean, expanded from Bangkok. Vietnam Tourism says the plates use local produce and imported ingredients, grilled on a wood-burning stove, with a wine list. Solo diners can sit at the bar. An upstairs room seats larger parties. No street number was printed.

spots.name: Baozi
spots.note: Taiwanese, in a room the page calls funky, hip, and modern. Founded by a Vietnamese-British man who brought a bao concept from London. The page says Taiwanese bao are open, unlike the closed Vietnamese bánh bao. The founder recommends scotch eggs, ramen, teriyaki ribs, pork belly rice, and the carrot cake. No street was printed.

spots.name: Anan Saigon
spots.note: Peter Cuong Franklin. Vietnam Tourism says the style is “Cuisine Moi,” French technique on Vietnamese street food, in the wet market, with a rooftop dining bar. The page calls it the place for a phở with a new perspective. The city itinerary also calls the room modern and elevated. It is filed once, in this chapter. No price was printed.

sections.heading: Themed dining
paragraphs: Rooms the pages describe by the setting: a rooftop, a sky bar, a brewery, a hotel bar, and the cafe buildings on Đồng Khởi and Nguyễn Huệ. No price was printed.

spots.name: Vo Roof Garden
spots.note: The city itinerary says modern Vietnamese dishes on a rooftop. No street was printed.

spots.name: L'Usine
spots.note: The city itinerary names L'Usine for a cold coffee on the Đồng Khởi shopping walk. No street number was printed.

spots.name: 42 Nguyen Hue
spots.note: The city itinerary, Visit HCMC, and the southern page name this former apartment block for cafes and shops. It is a building, not one restaurant.

spots.name: Do Phu Cafe
spots.note: Visit HCMC names Do Phu Café with sidewalk coffee at Turtle Lake and traditional cloth-filter coffee. No street was printed.

spots.name: Turtle Lake sidewalk coffee
spots.note: Visit HCMC names sidewalk coffee at Turtle Lake. No Vietnamese name for the lake, no street, and no clock were printed. The glass on the coffee page is not a photograph of this lake.

spots.name: Saigon Saigon Bar
spots.note: The city itinerary names Saigon Saigon Bar at the Caravelle. No price was printed.

spots.name: Pasteur Street Brewing Company
spots.note: The city itinerary names Pasteur Street Brewing Company. No street number and no price were printed.

spots.name: Glow Sky Bar
spots.note: The city itinerary names Glow Sky Bar. No street and no price were printed.

sections.heading: Breakfast
paragraphs: Cơm tấm is the breakfast Vietnam Tourism names, and the same page says people also eat it at any meal. The delicious-dishes page says the plate is breakfast, lunch, dinner, or supper, and that sticky rice is sold in the morning, at noon, in the afternoon, in the evening, and late at night. Bánh mì is the start of a morning on the city itinerary, and another page says it is sold at any hour. Cà phê sữa đá is the Saturday morning cup in the park outside the palace, before you go in.

spots.name: Cafes in the palace park
spots.note: The city itinerary puts cà phê sữa đá here on a Saturday morning. The cafes are not named. The coffee is not inside the palace ticket.

spots.name: Tan Dinh Market
spots.note: The city itinerary says Sunday morning produce, vegetables, and street-food snacks. The city itinerary places the market on Hai Bà Trưng in District 3. It is not Nhà thờ Tân Định.

seoTitle: Ho Chi Minh City food — cơm tấm, hủ tiếu, bánh tráng trộn
seoDescription: What the city pages name in Ho Chi Minh City: cơm tấm, hủ tiếu, bánh mì, bánh tráng trộn, bún bò Nam Bộ, xôi, and chè. Phở is best in Hanoi on the cuisine page, and a later page still describes a southern bowl.
